newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico's Fox eyes presidency with centrist plank.
newsitem.headline: Mexico's Fox eyes presidency with centrist plank.

text.p: Mexican state governor Vicente Fox said he is determined to swing the country's main right-wing opposition party to the ideological centre to help him achieve his ultimate goal -- the presidency in 2000.

With Mexico's governing Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI) looking shaky after historic losses in recent mid-term elections, Fox told Reuters he is the man who will end the PRI's 68-year hold on the nation's top post.
"I have no doubt I will be president," said the brash politician, comparing his task of unseating the PRI to that of putting a man on the moon -- difficult, but doable.

But the populist governor had little praise for his own National Action Party (PAN), saying it must adjust its ideological sails in order to catch the prevailing political winds and win the all-important 2000 race.

"There are things we need to fix in the PAN if we want to win in 2000. Today the PAN is going through a process, not unlike corporations or institutions, of re-engineering, restructuring and reinvention," Fox said late on Tuesday.
"The PAN has been misinterpreted to a certain extent ... It is not a right-wing party ... But it does need to move more to the centre," Fox said.

Although President Ernesto Zedillo's PRI lost control of Congress for the first time ever during the July 6 vote, the PAN came a disappointing third behind a growing leftist opposition that successfully wooed middle-class voters.

Sounding at times more like a card-carrying member of the leftist Party of the Democratic Revolution (PRD), Fox praised the PRD for moving to the middle and shedding its more radical ideas of the past. It placed second in Congress behind the PRI.
"The PAN used to get the PRI protest vote for free. Now we have competition. The PRD appears with a smart strategy ... places itself at centre-left and captures votes," he said.

Fox's prescription for the PAN is the same as the one he has used in his home state of Guanajuato: free-market with a heart. He has guaranteed free education through university to students with high marks and launched a credit programme for poor women based on a similar scheme in Bangladesh.
"We constantly underestimate the poor. All they need is an opportunity," said Fox, who along with his staff always wears a pin that reads: "Guanajuato: Land of Opportunity."

An admirer of U.S. President Bill Clinton and U.K. leader Tony Blair, both of whom moved their left-leaning parties to the centre, Fox said he was currently reading a book by Clinton's top former strategist Dick Morris.

The charismatic Fox, 54, is not your average Mexican politician. At 6-feet-4 (1.93 metres) he towers over his aides and eschews ties in favour of cowboy boots, jeans, and a belt-buckle branded with the name "Fox."

The son of a Spanish-born mother, the Guanajuato state governor is popular enough to have prompted Congress four years ago to overturn a constitutional ban on Mexicans with one or more foreign-born parents from becoming president.

Fox wants to bring his touch of populism to the PAN, which although seen as honest and efficient, suffers from an image that it is unsympathetic to the poor and at times as heavy-handed as the party it wants to replace.

In the central city of Aguascalientes in 1996, PAN officials closed an exhibition of photographs because it contained nude pictures. In Mexico's second city of Guadalajara, the PAN mayor tried to stop his female staff from wearing mini-skirts and imposed a curfew on young people.
The PAN, licking its wounds from the July 6 race, has already started to change, Fox said.

During a party convention last weekend, more orthodox PAN members like party head Felipe Calderon made room for a rival group of so-called "pragmatists" that is identified with Fox and other northern state governors.

That group, also known less affectionately as the "Barbarians of the North," will now be in charge of running the PAN's election campaigns and placed one of their own, Fox's predecesor in Guanajuato Carlos Medina Plasencia, as PAN leader in the lower house.
